S65: Husby parish register, male births 1855 — Niels Thomsen, born 9 July 1855, baptised in church 22 July. The parents’ column reads “Hmd. Øekjær Thomas Jensen og Hustru Anne Marie Jansdatter, 28 Aar” (smallholder, Øekjær, Thomas Jensen and his wife Anne Marie Jansdatter, 28 years). Among the godparents Niels Poulsgaard and Johanne Cathrine (wife of the smallholder Jesper Jensen — Jesper and Esper are the same name), Kirstine Hansdatter (daughter of the smallholder Peder Jensen), the girl Ane Marie Jensdatter and the bachelor Ole Jensen, “alle af Husby” (all of Husby). In the margin the name Silkjær has been added “ifl. Bevis 21/11 1905” (according to certificate 21/11 1905). The godparent “Johanne Cathrine, wife of the smallholder Jesper Jensen” can be identified through the district’s genealogical records (1uz.dk) as Johanne Cathrine Jensdatter, born in Øe in 1824, married on 16 March 1851 in Husby Church to Esper Jensen Klit — Thomas Jensen’s brother, cf. S69 — whose children were born in Øe; she died in January 1856. The husband is in all likelihood the Esper Jensen Ø. who survived the wreck of 1878, cf. S66. Whether the marginal endorsement of the name certificate also gives the issuing authority or a journal number has not been read. The date 21 November 1905 falls between two schemes — access to name certificates from the authorities under the royal resolution of 26 May 1903 ended on 1 July 1905, and the Names Act of 1904 was only in practical use from 1906 — so the basis on which the certificate was issued is unresolved; the certificate file itself has not been examined. Danish National Archives, Arkivalieronline

Sidst ere de blevne sete 4—5 Mil fra Land Løverdag 16 Juni om Eftermiddagen af Fiskerne paa et andet Fiskerskib fra Vedersø Klit, da disse efter endt Gjerning, kort før en frembrydende Sydøststorm, søgte Land. Baaden er i kantret Tilstand set drivende ved Hanstholm.” (These 5, together with the bachelor Jeppe Jensen of Nørfjand, put out with Jørgen Sørensen’s boat in the night between 15 and 16 June, but have not since come ashore, and must therefore be considered drowned. They were last seen 4—5 miles from land on Saturday 16 June in the afternoon by the fishermen of another boat from Vedersø Klit, who, their work done, were making for land shortly before a south-easterly gale broke. The boat has been seen drifting capsized off Hanstholm.) The register’s “2den Gang gift” agrees with the genealogical database’s two marriages (1851 and 1856). S117: Vridsløselille as an institution in 1913: the house of correction on Vridsløselille Mark (from 1933 Vridsløselille State Prison) was organised on the Philadelphia system — sentences served in solitary confinement day and night, a mask outside the cell, a ban on conversation and stalls in church and school; compulsory masks were only made voluntary in 1924, and the principle of isolation remained central until the Penal Code of 1930, in force in 1933. The Penal Code of 1866 at the same time laid down a reduction of the term for sentences served in solitary confinement — isolation was in itself considered an aggravating element — so that the actual time served by prisoners in the house of correction lay between 6 months and 3½ years, against sentences of 8 months to 6 years; the reduction was maintained until 1933. § 13 of the Act set the reduction at one third for the first three years; eighteen months of hard labour in the house of correction thereby became twelve, which corresponds exactly to the prison register’s date of release (27 April 1914, one year after the start of the sentence). The conversion has been checked against the text of the law; that the sentence was in fact served in solitary confinement is the law’s main rule and an inference from the date, not information in the prison register. The General Civil Penal Code of 10 February 1866, § 13 · Fængselshistorisk Selskab (Prison History Society), faengselshistorie.dk · kilderne.dk, the archive series Vridsløselille State Prison, register 1859—1932 · “Statsfængslet i Vridsløselille — del 1”, Nordisk Tidsskrift for Kriminalvidenskab, vol. 46, no. 4

Om blodskamssager og lovgivning før 1967” (When children were accomplices: on incest cases and legislation before 1967), Fynske Årbøger 2010 — a review of the incest legislation 1866—1933 and of Statistics Denmark’s figures: on average 26.2 people convicted of incest a year in the years around 1900 (the provision’s peak); around the turn of the century women made up about a third of those convicted in cases under §§ 161—162; after the age of criminal responsibility was raised to 14 in 1906, a total of 15 people between 14 and 18 were punished for incest in the whole country up to 1932; convicted daughters typically received eight months to a year in the house of correction, up to two years, and daughters whose “morality” was called into question were sentenced most harshly.
